deep.reconstruction:
This page is the continuation (n = 4300 to 9000) of the 'TABVLA exhibens valores litterarum N et M pro singulis valoribus litterae n' that begins on p. 382 and ends on p. 384. The page has no text, only the numerical table. Recomputing the entries shows they follow closed forms. With x = n/4000:
- M = 30(1 - e^{-x}).
- N = (4000/n)(1 - e^{-x}) = (1 - e^{-x})/x.
- Equivalently, M = 0.0075·n·N.

Checks:
- n = 4000 (previous page): N = 1 - 1/e = 0.6321, M = 18.963.
- n = 100: N = 40(1 - e^{-0.025}) = 0.9876, M = 0.7407.
- n = 9000: e^{-2.25} = 0.10540, so N = 0.3976, M = 26.838 (printed 26.8377).
- n = 40000 (next page): N = 0.1000, M → 30.

So M is a quantity that grows linearly (0.0075·n) for small n and saturates exponentially at the limit 30. N is the ratio of the actual value M to the value 0.0075·n it would have without the retarding effect, i.e. a 'reduction factor' (1 - e^{-x})/x.

This is exactly the profile produced by the linear first-order equation dM/dn = a - bM, with a = 0.0075 and b = 1/4000. Such an equation arises when a resistance proportional to v² acts and one integrates in terms of v² (the 'height due to the velocity'). Plausibly, in E260 this describes how fluid friction in a long tube or channel limits the velocity-height to a terminal value, compared with the frictionless value proportional to the length or fall. That physical reading is inferred from the numbers, not from text on this page. The table lets a practitioner read off how much friction reduces the outcome for a given length or height parameter n.
errors: Printed misprint at n = 5500: M is given as '2,24145'; the correct value is 22,4145 (30(1 - e^{-1.375}) = 22.4148), with the comma displaced.

The M column runs systematically low by about 2 to 6 units in the 4th decimal; for example n = 4300 gives 19.7611 computed vs 19.7605 printed, and n = 5200 gives 21.8240 vs 21.8234. The relative error in e^{-x} grows roughly linearly with x, about 5e-5·x. This is consistent with computing e^{-x} as 10^{-0.4343x} using a slightly truncated log10(e), or with an effective constant of about 4000.2 instead of 4000. It is a harmless computational artefact.
At n = 6900, M is printed as 24.6554, but computed it is 24.6548. This entry is off in the opposite direction to the systematic trend, so it is probably an isolated slip.

Several N entries are off by one unit in the last place. Computed vs printed: n = 6400: 0.4988 vs 0.4989; n = 6900: 0.4764 vs 0.4765; n = 7200: 0.4637 vs 0.4638; n = 7300: 0.4596 vs 0.4597; n = 7400: 0.4555 vs 0.4556; n = 7600: 0.4476 vs 0.4475; n = 8800: 0.4042 vs 0.4041; n = 5200: 0.5596 vs 0.5595. These are rounding or propagation effects.

ideas.what: Tabulation of the saturating solution M = A(1 - e^{-n/c}) and of the reduction factor N = (1 - e^{-n/c})/(n/c), for A = 30 and c = 4000.
ideas.modern_name: Exponential approach to a terminal value (solution of a linear first-order ODE); the function (1 - e^{-x})/x
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th-century technique (integration of dz/dx = a - bz); Euler and the Bernoullis used it routinely for resisted motion
ideas.where_published: E260 itself, Novi Commentarii Acad. Sci. Petrop. 6 (1756/57, publ. 1761); similar resisted-motion integrations appear in Euler's Mechanica (E15/E16) and in his ballistics work

ideas.what: Using a numerical table to show practitioners how strongly fluid friction reduces the frictionless result as a function of the size parameter n (the limit 30 is reached by n ≈ 55000).
ideas.modern_name: Engineering friction-loss table (precursor of pipe-flow loss tables of the Darcy–Weisbach type)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Pipe-friction empirics are usually credited to Chézy (1770s), Prony, Darcy (1857) and Weisbach (1845)

deep.surprise_reason: A routine numerical table of 30(1 - e^{-n/4000}) and its ratio to the linear value. Its reconstruction is straightforward, and it contains only small computational slips and one misprint. No new mathematics or overlooked connection is on this page.
